utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; and Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else in the courtroom. We're in Courtroom II today, although it seems that Courtroom I and III are available. But unfortunately we've been given this courtroom, which is fine, but it would have been better to have a bigger courtroom. I note that there are only five seats for the Defence, and usually there are six members of the Defence team. Unfortunately, there is no possibility for a sixth lawyer to be present. If we had our model, we wouldn't be able to have the hearing here with the model. And Mr. Withopf, as far as the model is concerned, have you seen the model and has the Prosecution any comments to make about the model?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, to date I haven't seen the model yet, but the Prosecution is in contact with Defence, and this issue will be sorted out very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. But if we had a model in this courtroom, it would have to be a lot smaller. We have three witnesses scheduled for the hearing. I think that they are present. They are international monitors. And naturally, their testimony will be very interesting and very important. The Trial Chamber would like to indicate immediately that we reserve the right to ask these witnesses technical questions if the Prosecution and the Defence haven't asked questions which might be of importance and relevance. Without wasting any more time, since I know that it might take time to examine these witnesses, we'll call the first witness into the courtroom. Could the usher go and fetch the first witness. Unless there is something that Mr. Bourgon would like to say before the witness is called into the courtroom. Yes, go ahead then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours. The Defence would like to raise an issue before the beginning of the testimony or after the testimony. This concerns the documents from the ECMM. Mr. President, we can deal with this matter now, immediately, or after the testimony is given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's best to do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have conferred with our colleagues from the Prosecution about the documents briefly. The problem is that we received a number of documents which come from the archives in Sarajevo. We have also received a certificate according to which these documents are all the ones located in Sarajevo. But it seems that we have certain documents provided to us by the Prosecution, yet we didn't find these documents in Sarajevo. For this reason, we are concerned and we would like to know where the other documents are. We would like to know how the Prosecution managed to obtain these documents. We have identified a mechanism, a procedure today, that would enable us to obtain these documents. Firstly, the Prosecution has said that they will provide us with a list of all the documents that they have in their possession and which corresponds to the criteria identified in Annex B of our request which was filed in December. So with this list, we should be in a position to inform the Prosecution of the documents that they have and that we don't have, documents that could be provided to us at a subsequent date. This procedure relates to two permits given by the EU. First of all, the Prosecution could disclose the list of documents to us. And second of all, the Prosecution would be authorised to disclose the documents in question, the ones that we don't have in our possession. The reason for which the Defence would like to deal with this matter today, to discuss this matter today, is that the first witness from the ECMM should be testifying next Friday, on the 29th of March. Mr. President, we believe that it is important to be able to obtain all the documents before the first witness is heard. According to my colleagues from the Prosecution, it should be possible to obtain the two authorisations and the documents in good time. We should have sufficient time to consult the documents before this witness testifies on Friday, the 29th. We simply wanted to raise this issue before the Trial Chamber and we hope that we'll be able to resolve the problem so that we aren't late when it comes to the testimony of the witnesses from the EU -- the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf will respond to these issues. But if the permission arrives too late, then a solution would be to hear the witness scheduled for Friday, the 29th at a later date. But Mr. Withopf will certainly provide us with additional explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I can confirm that today Defence and Prosecution had a meeting discussing this issue in detail. The ECMM documents stem from three different sources. The vast majority stems obviously from ECMM; the second source is the Danish Foreign Ministry; and the third source is a number -- are a number of witnesses who provided the Prosecution with a number of ECMM documents. The Prosecution was able to find out a way to efficiently deal with the request made by Defence counsel recently. We are talking about some 10.000 of documents. The list in respect to 7.000 out of the about 10.000 documents can be made available very soon. It's a pure technical issue, and the Prosecution can deal with it. More complex, however, appears to be the issue of the ECMM granting the lifting of the Rule 70 restrictions. I will contact ECMM at the very earliest opportunity to discuss this issue with them, provided that they are prepared to lift the Rule 70 restrictions, Defence counsel will receive the respective lists in the near future. And it appears - however, a guarantee can obviously not be given - but it appears to be realistic that the list can be provided prior to the first ECMM witness appearing before this Court. The first one is scheduled to testify Thursday, 1st of April and Friday, 2nd of April. If I may use this opportunity to also inform the Trial Chamber that today the Prosecution will disclose a number of Rule 68 documents stemming from the ECMM collection. In that respect, ECMM has been given -- has given the permission to disclose such materials. Thank you very much. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf, for this information. Naturally, the Trial Chamber will listen to what the parties have to say about this issue, and please don't hesitate to take stock of the matter as soon as necessary. And if necessary, file motions with us. Naturally, Defence should have access to these documents so that they can conduct their defence and be familiar with the documents that are relevant. I'm now going to ask the usher to bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. Are you hearing what I'm saying interpreted into your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called here as a witness for the Prosecution. Before you testify, you should make a solemn declaration. But before you do so, you should first tell me your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Vaughan Kent-Payne.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 13th of October, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which town were you born in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Beverly, in the County of East Yorkshire, in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your position and what is your current rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a major in the -- in the British Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What position and rank did you have in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a major and an infantry company commander in the 1st Battalion, the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment, Yorkshire Battle Group in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you already testified in court with regard to the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You should now make the solemn declaration. Could you please read out the text that you'll be shown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the Prosecution starts with its examination-in-chief, I would like to provide you with some information about the procedure followed in this courtroom. You will first have to answer questions that will be put to you by representatives of the Prosecution. The representatives of the Prosecution are to your right. And when conducting the examination-in-chief, they will ask you about events of which you were an eyewitness in 1993. Once they have concluded their examination-in-chief, Defence counsel, who are to your left, will conduct their cross-examination. The questions that they put to you will be somewhat different from the ones put to you by the Prosecution, given that the purpose of their questions will be to check your credibility as a witness and also to ask you questions that have to do with the general context at the time. So you'll have to answer such questions. In addition, the three Judges, who are sitting before you, may ask you questions at any point in time. But given that you were an international observer at the time - and you will testify about this - we might ask you questions that haven't been put to you by either of the parties if we think that it's necessary to obtain additional information about the facts that you witnessed. Pay careful attention to the questions that are put to you. If a question seems to be complicated or unclear to you, ask the person who is putting the question to you to rephrase it. Before you answer a question, think about your answer, especially if the questions are complicated. If you don't understand the meaning of a question, ask the person putting the question to you to rephrase it, to make sure that the question is very clear to you. As I have already said, Defence counsel will also ask you a series of questions, and they will also make an attempt to ask you clear and precise questions. They will avoid asking you questions -- asking you lengthy questions. The Trial Chamber will be monitoring all the questions put to you. There are two other things I would like to inform you of: As you have sworn to speak the truth, naturally you are not to lie, because if you have made a solemn declaration and give false testimony, in such a case the witness who has given false testimony could be prosecuted. Such a witness could be fined or could be given a prison sentence or both penalties could be imposed on the witness. In addition - but this doesn't concern you - a witness when answering questions might provide information that could be used against the witness at a subsequent date. If that is the case, the witness can refuse to answer the question. This is a well-known principle in Anglo-Saxon law. But nevertheless, if the Trial Chamber wants to compel the witness to answer the question, what the witness says when answering the question can't be used against him. So this is how the hearing will proceed. I believe that the Prosecution has already provided you with some information about the proceedings. And as I see that you are a professional soldier, you should be quite familiar with proceedings in military courts. And roughly speaking, it should be similar to the proceedings in this court. So you should not -- you probably won't be losing your bearings here. Without wasting any more time, I will now let the Prosecution commence with their examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President, good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, can you please for the benefit of the Trial Chamber briefly describe your military career with respect to various postings and assignments that you've had.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: I was commissioned as an officer in 1978 and joined United Kingdom infantry battalion as a commander in charge of 30 soldiers, where I spent two years, including a tour of duty in Belfast, Northern Ireland. I then spent two years at a recruits' training depot training young soldiers before returning to my regiment as the reconnaissance platoon commander in Berlin in the days before the wall came down. I then returned to Northern Ireland for two years as the battalion operations officer, planning operations at battalion level before going to our non-commissioned officers training school for two years. In 1990, I attended the army staff course. And from 1991 to 1992, I was the chief of staff of a brigade and operations in Northern Ireland. I spent three years as a rifle company commander, including the United Nations tour of Bosnia in 1993, before spending six months as an operations officer in the operational headquarters in the Falkland Islands. From 1996 to 1999, I was based in the Middle East instructing the Kuwaiti armed forces on the use of British equipment before returning to my battalion as second-in-command in 1999 for two years including two duties -- two tours of duty in Northern Ireland. In 2001, I spent 6 months as the chief operations officer of a multinational brigade in Pristina, in Kosovo, followed by six months as a United Nations military observer in Sierra Leone. I then spent eight Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. months as the chief of staff of British forces in the Balkans, based in Banja Luka, in Northern Bosnia. And my last job has been the United Kingdom peace-keeping advisor to the Economic Community of West African States, ECOWAS, based in Nigeria, and planning the West African peace-keeping operations in Cote d'Ivoire and Liberia. I took over my present appointment as chief instructor at our officer training school about ten days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Major Kent-Payne, you mentioned being involved with the United Nations in Bosnia in 1993. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber when you first went to Bosnia and for what purpose.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: It was in February 1993, on the reconnaissance party for my regiment, the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment of Yorkshire. The commanding officer, the company commanders, and the principal staff officers spent one week in Vitez in Central Bosnia with the previous battalion, the Cheshire Regiment, in order to familiarise ourselves with the area, the procedures for United Nations peace-keeping operations, so that we could go back to our unit in Germany and supervise the training and briefing of our own soldiers prior to deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major, when in fact did you first then deploy back to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: It was around the 15th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, when did your unit deploy to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: The soldiers deployed in a series of flights over the period of about two weeks, and we assumed command of the operational area on about the 9th or 10th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major, what did you do between the period when you deployed to Bosnia around the 15th of April, 1993 and when your unit joined you and you assumed the operational area on or about the 9th or 10th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: We spent approximately three weeks carrying out familiarisation patrols with the previous battalion. This involved travelling around the area, getting to know the area, getting to know the operational procedures, and meeting some of the local commanders in a series of meetings. Our own vehicles then arrived, and we took time to prepare these to do final training before my own company went on to a few days' guard duties, and we assumed operation control of our area on about the 11th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned your vehicles arriving. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what type of vehicles your unit had when you were in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: I was responsible for "C" Company group - that's C, the letter C - and I commanded some 30 armoured vehicles. Fourteen of these were Warrior infantry armoured personnel carriers. These are a tracked vehicle of about 30 tonnes armed with a 30-millimetre cannon; four small Scimitar light tanks, which weigh about 10 tonnes, also tracked; and a number of other tracked armoured vehicles from our support weapons platoon, the anti-tank platoons, and the mortar platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, you told us that you commanded "C" Company. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber the way your unit, meaning your larger unit, your regiment, was structured at the time you were in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: The way we were structured were three infantry companies, otherwise known as rifle companies, lettered A, B, and C; a support weapons company with anti-tank mortars and reconnaissance assets; and a headquarters company, with the administrative elements. For the purposes of this tour, we also had attached to us "C" Squadron of the Light Dragoons and Reconnaissance Regiment with Scimitar light tanks. For this tour, we were -- the support company was split between the various rifle companies and the armoured squadron, so we had four deployable subunits, each of around 150 to 200 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did your regiment remain in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: The regiment as a whole remained there for six months. Some individuals such as myself who went on the first advance party and left on the last flight were there for a total of seven months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the structure that you've just told us about, in terms of the different companies, remain the same throughout that tour, or did it change at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: The structure remained the same; although, the locations of the -- of the companies did change to some extent. And my own company, "C" Company, remained in Vitez throughout the duration of the tour. The -- our own "B" Company remained in Gornji Vakuf throughout the duration of the tour. However, the light dragoon squadron and our "A" Company swapped over for a period up in Tuzla, to the north of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where in Vitez was the "C" Company garrisoned?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: We were garrisoned in -- in Vitez school, which is approximately 3 kilometres outside the town of Vitez. It was a -- a primary school which had been taken over for the duration of the UN operations and rented from the local authorities by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us that the "A" Company swapped over for a period, the light dragoon squadron and the "A" Company swapped over for a period up in Tuzla. Were those -- either of those units deployed anywhere other than Tuzla? And if so, can you please tell where you say they were.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes. At the start of our tour, "A" Company and my own company, "C" Company, were in Vitez. And then after about three months, "A" Company went up to Tuzla swapping over with the light dragoons for approximately two months. And then for the last four to six weeks of the tour they swapped over again and then the light dragoons returned up to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just ask either the usher or the technical booth if they could lower the boom on the ELMO. It might be easier for me to see the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major, can you please tell the Trial Chamber who commanded the "A" and "B" Companies during this deployment to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: "A" Company was commanded by Major Roy Hunter and "B" Company by Major Graham Binns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, during the deployment can you please tell the Trial Chamber to whom you reported, that is your chain of command going upwards?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: My chain of command up was to the battalion commanding officer, Lieutenant Colonel Alistair Duncan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall who Lieutenant Colonel Duncan reported to?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Colonel Duncan reported to the brigade commander, who for the first four or five months of the tour was Brigadier Robin Searby, and for the last six weeks possibly of the tour was Brigadier John Reeth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, can you please describe what the terms of reference or mission of your unit was during the time you were deployed to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: The mission that we were given by the United Nations was quite clear, which was to escort humanitarian aid convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time that your unit was deployed in Bosnia, did that mission change or somehow evolve?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: The mission itself did not change, but the previous commanding officer, Lieutenant Colonel Bob Stewart, and my own commanding officer did what we call in the military a process called mission analysis, which is to look at the task and see whether the way that we're doing it is the best way to carry out the task. And what they decided was that the only way to successfully move humanitarian aid convoys was if the area was peaceful. And so we went from being convoy escorts to in effect peace-keepers. And although the United Nations mandate did not allow us to peace in force, then what we were able to do was to negotiate peace by whatever means possible to ensure the area was as quiet as possible, to therefore move or convoys with the minimum amount of escorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major, can you please tell the Trial Chamber what steps you took in order to familiarise yourself with the area of responsibility of your company.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: First of all, the company commanders had all been around the area on our reconnaissance and had briefed our soldiers accordingly. However, when we arrived in Bosnia in April, the areas had changed somewhat due to the withdrawing of the United Nations boundaries. So we therefore had to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. set out to travel as much of the area of possible. For the first three weeks, we did this in company with soldiers from the previous battalion. And then for our first week or ten days, once our own vehicles had arrived from Germany, we sent out patrols with the soldiers and the junior commanders to various areas so they could get to know both the villages and the routes that led to these particular villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you describe, please, for the Trial Chamber the area of responsibility that your company patrolled

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Roughly in the north of the area our northern boundary was the front line with the Serbs, which was in the area of Zepce and Maglaj. To the west our boundary again was the front line with the Bosnian Serbs in the area of Turbe. To the south, our boundary was an imaginary point which was a map reference, which -- in which we bounded onto our "B" Company, the Gornji Vakuf company. Roughly speaking, this was mid-way between Novi Travnik and Gornji Vakuf. And in the east, our boundary was basically the Sarajevo to Zenica road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how many men were in your company during this time period?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: On an average, 210.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please briefly describe some of the geographic features, villages, and towns that were located within your company's area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: The -- as I've said, the battalion was based in Vitez school, which was about 3 kilometres from Vitez. And our administrative elements were based in a disused garage, which was approximately 1 kilometre from Vitez. The main cities in the area were Zenica, which was to the north-east; Travnik, which was to the west; Novi Travnik, which was slightly south of that; and then smaller towns, Busovaca and Kiseljak, to the south-east; and, of course, Vitez itself. The two main features were the Vlasic Mountain feature, which overlooked Travnik, which in this time was held by the Serbs; and the river valley of the Lasva River, which ran roughly east to west through our area. There were very few roads through the area. Indeed, to get to Zenica there were only three possible roads then, and many of the smaller tracks were either impassable to our Warrior armoured vehicles or at least very difficult going, particularly in bad weather.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you arrived in late April, followed shortly thereafter by the -- your company, what were the weather conditions like in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: As spring had just arrived, the snow had -- had melted and disappeared, and the -- and the weather was just starting to become warm. When we were there in February, there was quite deep snow on the road, and this obviously clearly prevented much patrolling, particularly on some of the smaller tracks and into the mountainous areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did that snow that you observed in February when you were on your reconnaissance mission, did that in any way affect the Cheshire Regiment, your predecessor regiment, in terms of their operations in the area?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: It had a significant effect on their operations, to the point where they were only able to -- to patrol on the main roads and immediately off the main roads. There was no system of local authority snowploughs. We had no snowploughs ourselves. And despite the vehicles being tracked, they're still prone to sliding around in icy conditions. And indeed the Cheshires had some serious vehicle accidents problems which caused their commanding officer to curtail much of their patrolling. What this meant was that for most of the area there was no patrolling into some of the smaller villages whatsoever, not through any fault of the regiment, but simply due to the adverse weather conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what effect, if any, did the curtailment of these patrols have on their ability to obtain information?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: It meant that most of the area that wasn't immediately accessible by a main road was basically a complete void of information then, and any information that did come from these areas was generally by word of mouth or hearsay but with no actual UN eyes on the grounds to see for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major, can you please describe or provide some information to the Trial Chamber about the types of patrols that you undertook after your company was on the ground in Bosnia, beginning in May upon their arrival, May 1993.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: The way we operated was that in Vitez with the two companies there, one company would be the guard company, and their responsibilities were clearly guarding our own camp and the perimeter of our camp with sentries and static positions, with roving sentries, i.e., walking round, with a quick reaction force, and also any other permanent static duties that we were tasked to employ. The second company was the patrol company, and this was mainly responsible for convoy es courts -- escorts, the movement of local commanders from one place to the other, escorts of officially accredited aid agencies, such as the UNHCR, and indeed, if possible, some escort of some of the non-governmental organisations, such as the International Red Cross and Medecins Sans Frontieres. The remaining vehicle corps signs, of which there could be a minimum of two or a maximum of six, would then be tasked by myself, the company commander, on advice from the battalion operations and intelligence officers to various locations with a typical task being to go to a village to assess its -- its need of UN food aid, to go to a village to find out the exact locations of the front line or other such military information tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, can you please the Trial Chamber -- can you tell the Trial Chamber some of the villages or areas that you began patrolling in mid-May 1993.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: The first places that we went to were places where we'd not been able to go to before and where the -- where the Cheshires had little or no information on these villages. The system that we employed was a system called the honesty trace, which was where each time you came back off a patrol you filed a tracing paper map overlay of where you'd been and these were kept on record in the battalion headquarters. Simply by looking through these records - bear in mind it was the days before the current use of IT and computer equipment, by going through these records you were able to see what had been visited and what had been found out in these particular areas. So we started to -- to attempt first to go to the villages that had seen no UN presence. One of the main reasons for this was to show a UN presence throughout our area, to reassure the local population that the United Nations was not simply confined to the main roads but had free access to all of the areas, as agreed by the various parties with the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall some of these villages that hadn't been visited prior to the arrival of your unit, some of the areas where you did in fact go?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Basically anything in the Bila Valley and north of the village of Han Bila, which had been cut off by the weather, anything in the hills to the south of Kiseljak, anything to the north of the hills around Busovaca. Basically the areas of high ground that had not been visited before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, do you recall the first time your unit went up into the Bila Valley and the area north of Han Bila?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes. We'd been tasked on two or three occasions to go into the area of Han Bila for prisoner exchanges. There was a small sort of detention centre there, and we were involved in some prisoner exchanges. And also the route through Han Bila was the back way from Vitez into Zenica via a road through some small villages in the hills. However, in the middle of May, about the 15th of May, I was tasked to patrol to the north of Han Bila in order to assess the aid situation in three villages. Please excuse my pronunciation, called Suhi Dol, Has [phoen], and Rat [phoen]. And also, because these areas were relatively close to the Serb front lines in the Vlasic feature, to ask the local people there whether they'd seen any Serbian soldiers and what they believed the state of the front line to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber what happened as you and your soldiers went up the Bila Valley on 15 May 1993.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: At the bottom of the Bila Valley at the Vitez end was a Croat checkpoint. By "Croat" I mean Bosnian Croat. And they obligingly moved their -- and their anti-tank mines out of the way to let us through. And we proceeded up the valley, basically making map corrections to our maps and improving our knowledge of the area, until we reached the village of Han Bila. There we were stopped by a small group of BiH - Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina - militia men who stood in front of us and indicated that they wouldn't let us pass. At this stage there was no barrier, simply the presence of armed soldiers in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major, if I could just interrupt for one moment. Approximately what time of day was it that you arrived at this checkpoint where the BiH soldiers were?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: This would have been about 9.45, 10.00 in the morning, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately how many men and how many vehicles were in your group on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: In my patrol, I had two Warrior armoured personnel carriers, each with five crew; two turret crew, a commander and a gunner, a driver, and two soldiers in the back, who would act as -- act as protection to look to the sides of the vehicle and the rear of the vehicle. And we were also carrying a young female local interpreter as well, who was on her first -- her first job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry for interrupting, but can you please then continue and tell the Trial Chamber what happened after you arrived at this checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: I dismounted from my vehicle with my interpreter and went forward to speak to the local militia men and explained that we were with the United Nations, they had no right to stop us from going along this road. The -- the right of passage of the United Nations had been agreed between their high command and the United Nations and they should let us pass. The local militiamen said that I should speak to their local commander, and I was ushered into a small building by the side of the track, where we waited for 10 or 15 minutes and some coffee was brought to us. In the building, I had myself, my close protection NCO, which is a military euphemism for bodyguard, if you like, and the young female interpreter. After about 15 minutes the local commander arrived, who was a man in his early 60s, I suppose, and was clearly local militia, rather than a front line infantry soldier. And we talked for approximately 30 to 40 minutes. I explained why we wanted to go to these villages, the purpose of us being there, and I tried to show that it would be to the benefit of the local population to allow me to go there, to assess the aid situation with a view to possibly getting humanitarian aid to those villages at a later date. However, he was not compliant in letting us past, and it was clear after about 40 minute that is we were not going to be allowed to pass this. And from our mandate, clearly, although we did have free passage of movement, there was no question of forcing this because frankly the task wasn't worth -- wasn't worth hurting anyone to -- to carry out. After about 40 minutes, just as we were about to give up and turn around and go away, another man came into the room, whispered something to the local commander, who then said that he'd had the orders from his high command and that we would be allowed to proceed up the track to the north of Han Bila, as we'd requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major, again, I apologise for interrupting. Let me ask a couple of follow-on questions: The local commander that you've just described for us in Han Bila, what was he wearing on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: As I recall, he was wearing combat fatigue trousers and a -- a green -- a green T-shirt and a camouflage waistcoat of the same material. In the early stage of our tour, particularly the BiH had not adopted much of rank structure and they didn't have unit identification badges, and actually, there was nothing really to tell a BiH soldier apart from a -- an HVO Croat soldier other than sometimes the Croat soldiers wore red-and-white chequer-board badge on their sleeve. And so there was no way of looking at this man and saying yes, this is the local commander. Unlike us - I'm wearing rank badges - they didn't do that. He simply announced himself as the local commander and we had no reason to doubt his word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, the people, the persons you've described as manning the checkpoints in this community, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: They again were wearing a mixture of an American-style fatigue uniform and civilian clothes. It was quite -- it was not that common to see people in full military uniform. Each soldier wore either a -- either a shirt or trousers but rarely both. But they would normally wear something to indicate that they were not just a normal civilian. They were armed with a variety of weapons. When we first arrived there, there was simply three or four AK-47-type assault rifles. By the time I emerged from the building after close to an hour, this had been swelled by the addition of some hand-held anti-tank weapons and a couple of machine-guns as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was your interpreter that you had with you able to communicate with the persons at the checkpoint and the local commander?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes, she was. Although, she was only 18 or 19 years old and had only learned English at school. Then she became more adept as the -- as the conversation wore on. Interpreting is a skill. It's not something you can pick up straight away. But as we went on, she became better. And it was also the first time that I'd used an interpreter, so I learned to speak more slowly and clearly and not to use too many military-type words, which she wouldn't have had course to learn in the -- in the course of her studies at school. But yes, she was communicating with -- with the locals and they had a small discussion about -- about where they came from and families and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Major, I've just been passed a note to in fact ask you to speak a little bit more slowly here in the courtroom. My question, I guess, with respect to the interpreter went more towards the language spoken by the local commander and the soldiers at the checkpoint. Was she able to understand them? Were they speaking a common language --

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- to the best of what you were able to observe.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes. By this stage, we had -- we, the British, had picked up a small and rudimentary grasp of Serbo-Croat. And it was clear that they were speaking, the interpreter and the local commander, were speaking in Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's resume where you were when I interrupted you. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber how you then proceeded from this checkpoint, where you went next.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Once the local commander gave us permission to move forward, I returned to my vehicle, noticing that the crowd of people had swelled to around 30 or 40 local militia and around 100 civilians just watching what was going on. Then -- and bear in mind that it was quite unusual for these people to see a UN vehicle at this stage, so we were something of a novelty. The atmosphere was friendly, almost carnival-like, and it was clear that most of these people were -- were locals from the village of Han Bila. We shook a few hands and exchanged farewells and got into our vehicles and started to drive north and up the road along the -- along the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I neglected to ask you earlier, Major, what colour were your vehicles?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: White, and at this stage because those vehicles had come straight from Germany and straight from being repainted, they were a very, very bright white indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. You've told us now that you drove north along the road along the Bila Valley. How far north did you drive on that day?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: We drove for about 6 kilometres or so, with the intention of moving into a village called Fazlici and then turning left on a small track, which was marked on the map, and heading for the village of Suhi Dol. However, just before we reached Fazlici, we came to a stoutly-constructed checkpoint. And by that I mean there was a proper -- a proper barrier across the road which could be lifted up and a properly constructed guardhut with wooden walls, roof, and small windows. And this was something that we hadn't seen before. Most of the checkpoints were simply a log across the road, an oil drum, or something like that. But this was actually a properly constructed and seemed to have been there for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately what time on May 15th, 1993 did you arrive at this checkpoint near Fazlici?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: This would have been around about midday at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major, I also neglected to ask you what time you left your garrison on that morning on this journey up the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: As with most of the patrol, we would have left between 9.00 and -- 9.00 and 9.15 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what happened at the checkpoint that you arrived at near Fazlici at midday on 15 May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: The -- the barrier across the road was down. And from the top of my vehicle, I indicated for it to be lifted. And the soldier on duty on the barrier shook his head. It was clear that he was not going to let us through, so I dismounted from the vehicle and went forward with my close protection soldier and the interpreter. We talked to the soldier on duty at the barrier, and he then sent someone off to fetch his local commander. And another Bosnian Muslim arrived, wearing BiH uniform jacket and trousers, and he told us that we were not allowed to proceed any further north without papers signed by the headquarters of 3 Corps. Now, at this stage we had been briefed by the United Nations that free passage for United Nations vehicles had been negotiated with the warring parties and that under no circumstances were we to agree to go and fetch any piece of paper from any military commander. And the purpose of this was to do so would be to admit that the military leadership of the HVO and the BiH had some control over where the United Nations went, and clearly that was outside the agreement that had been made. So I re refused to do this, to get a piece of paper, and we talked for approximately 15 minutes, during which time it became clear that he was not going to let us through the checkpoint and we had no authority to force our way through this checkpoint. The task that we were doing was not to save life, so clearly to injure someone in the process or to damage property would have been an escalation of the situation, which we did not want to do. Having realised we were not going to get through the checkpoint, we just started to talk about the weather, about football, and just to generally pass the time of day. And I asked him some questions about the Serbs and the state of the war, and everything was friendly. By this stage, the group of local militia had swelled to about 15 or 20. The soldiers had their rifles slung over their shoulders, and there was nothing threatening or aggressive about the situation whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, approximately how long did you remain at this checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: We were there for about 30 minutes, and I was just at the point of saying thank you very much, we will come back at another day perhaps with the piece of paper you've asked for when a -- a white Toyota pick-up arrived at high speed. And out of this got a -- an individual who was wearing combat trousers and a green T-shirt and a camouflage combat waistcoat. And from my initial view of him, he appeared to be of North African extraction, perhaps from the area of the Horn of Africa, Ethiopia, Somalia. And he didn't speak any Serbo-Croat that I heard, but he shouted to the local militia men and prodded at them in an -- in an aggressive gesture with his AK-47 rifle. The local militia immediately took their weapons off their shoulders, cocked them - that is to say, pulled the working parts to load a bullet into the chamber of the rifle, therefore making sure that it could fire - and he gesticulated from side to side to make them deploy onto the high ground on the side of the vehicles in what was definitely an escalation of the situation and a more threatening posture from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major, if I could ask just a couple of questions. When you say that this was an escalation of the situation and a more threatening posture from them, towards whom was this escalation directed?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: The -- the threat was clearly against myself and my vehicles and their crew. Then at this stage the -- the turret and the gun on our vehicles were pointing to the front. I deliberately ensured that we did not move the turret from side to side, which would look aggressive, then. And we were simply sitting in the middle of the road, two large white vehicles. With myself standing out of the front of the vehicle, to all intents and purposes unarmed, as my own weapon, a pistol, was underneath my flak jacket and could not be seen from the outside. So it was definitely an escalation from their part and not provoked on any count by any of our actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major, you told us that the turrets of the Warriors were pointed to the front. Where in relation to the vehicles were -- were you standing at the time you were speaking to the local commander when this white Toyota arrived?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: I was standing about 30 metres in front of the -- front of the Warrior, and the procedure we had adopted was that the -- the vehicle would not stop directly in front of the checkpoint but some 30 to 40 metres to the rear, which would give some room for manoeuvre should the vehicle have to turn round or surge forward or go to the rear. It would also mean that because the gun of the vehicle can only go down, can only depress so far, that they would have a chance to use the weapon, given the additional distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also told the Chamber that the individual who got out of the Toyota pick-up appeared to you to be North African or from the Horn of Africa. What did you base that assessment on?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Well, my first impression was clearly he was -- he was most unlikely to be a Bosnian and he didn't look like a Bosnian. He was much darker-skinned. He had -- had North African features, closely -- close cropped curly hair, black curly hair. And also the fact that he quite clearly was shouting something which most definitely wasn't Serbo-Croat. And the interpreter said to me, "I can't understand what he's saying." So -- so I knew he wasn't a Bosnian, and I assumed from seeing people on the television from Somalia that he was from that part of Africa, North Africa certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What happened after this individual got out of the white pick-up?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: I was concentrating on him and what he was doing. He -- he refused to talk to me, and so because the situation had escalated I walked to the rear of my vehicle and one of my soldiers handed me my rifle, which I then cocked in the back of the vehicle out of sight of the -- of the local militia. And my close protection NCO, who was carrying a light machine-gun - also cocked - unloaded his weapon. We then returned to the front of the vehicle with the interpreter and back to the barrier. During this time, a second man got out of the pick-up and came towards the barrier. He was most definitely an Arab or certainly appeared to be. He was around 5 foot 4 inches tall with a closely trimmed beard which was slightly greying and slightly greying at the temples, and he had what I can only describe as cold, hard eyes. I held out my hand to him, and in my rudimentary Serbo-Croat said, "Doba dan, kako ste? Ja se zovem Major Vaughan," "Hello, how are you, my name is Major Vaughan." Because the interpreter was on her first day at work, she repeated the sentence as well, much to everyone's confusion. The Arab gentleman refused to shake my hand and said to me in very good English, "I will not shake the hand of an infidel and I will not talk to you with a woman present." As he clearly spoke English that I could understand, I sent the interpreter back to the vehicle to get in the back, which was much to her relief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you then enter into a discussion with this individual who spoke English to you?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes. I again talked to him and asked that we be allowed to proceed through that checkpoint to the various villages that are discussed. I told him why we were there. I reminded him that they had no right to stop the United Nations and that we were not interfering in the civil war. We were simply there to assess the situation and report back as to whether the humanitarian aid was needed in these villages. And I pointed out to him that it was in the interest of him and his people to let us through. And -- however, he was having none of this and said that we -- that we were foreigners in his country, in the country, and that the -- that he and the other Muslims would look after the Bosnian Muslims and that they didn't need the United Nations to be there. And we discussed this for about 25 or 30 minutes, during which time it became increasingly apparent that he was not going to let me through his checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Payne, at the time you were discussing these issues with this individual, were you able to hear anything else that was going on around you?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, when -- when we were carrying out negotiations, we'd been taught to look the person that you were talking with directly in the eye, then, so you could gauge whether he was telling the truth, whether he was lying, whether he was excited, nervous, or whatever. And that was one of the main reasons why we had a close protection NCO to keep an eye on what was going on around us, because our whole attention as the commander was focussed onto their commander. During this time, my bodyguard was whispering to me that more and more people were coming. And at a break in the conversation, I looked around and saw that the crowd of people had grown to at this stage well over 100. A mixture of both local militia, people who were quite clearly Bosnian, and 30 to 40 foreigners, including some black men, a large number of Arabs, and people of other nationalities. They were better equipped than the local militia, had heavier weapon, had anti-tank weapons, and had -- had more uniform between them. And my attention was grabbed by someone suddenly shouting, "Death to the infidels" in English, but not just in English but in a broad Yorkshire accent, which is a region of England which I'm from and where all the soldiers from my battalion are from. And this was very incongruous in the middle of Bosnia to hear a man from a foreign military organisation insulting us, calling us unbelievers in our own language of English, then. I turned to the crowd but was not able to identify him in the crowd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what these people that you saw, this crowd of more than 100 people gathered around you, what they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: The -- the majority were wearing military-style combat uniform or at least part of this. When we initially arrived at the checkpoint, there were a number of women and children there, but these were ushered to the back and then away, almost as if something was going to happen and no one wanted them to be in the firing line. The weapons that they were carrying were all of former Soviet type, AK-47 rifles, 64-millimetre, and anti-tank weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, just a few moments ago, Major Kent-Payne, you mentioned "they were better equipped than the local militia." When you used the word "they," to whom were you referring?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: At this stage, all I could tell was that these were clearly foreigners. They weren't -- they weren't Bosnians. Not many Bosnians have Yorkshire accents. There were clearly some Arabs there and some -- some black men, possibly from Africa, then. So these were clearly not the normal Bosnian -- Bosnia militia. Then when I say "better equipped," a lot of the local militia had either bolt-action rifles or old semiautomatic rifles of the SKS pattern; whereas, the -- as I refer to them, the foreigners had -- had more modern AK-47-type weapons, light machine-guns, and anti-tank weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, approximately how long in total did you remain at this checkpoint near Fazlici?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: We were there for approximately 100 minutes to 2 hours, I suppose, all told. After I'd clearly realised that the Arabic gentleman was not going to let us through, he then changed the subject and started to berate me for being a member of the United Nations. He said what was I doing in the country as an outsider. He asked if I knew what the five pillars of Islam were, and he said that Islam was the only true religion and that the West was decadent and the United Nations was part of the West and was therefore decadent too and would -- would not be able to solve the problems in Central Bosnia. And I listened to this for about 15 or 20 minutes, and it was all becoming a little boring at this stage. And I then noticed that to my left and right the -- the local militia and the foreigners had spread out and were almost completely encircling us. And this I judged to be exceptionally threatening then, and I decided I was going to disengage from the situation because it was clear that it was leading up to either them or us shooting, and this was way beyond the scope of what we'd been asked to do. So I said to the Arab man that "We are the United Nations. We are peaceful, and we mean you no harm. We are not here to threaten you." And at that stage my vehicle gunner inside my -- my Warrior, about 30 metres behind me, clearly decided that the situation was extremely threatening and he loaded six rounds of high explosive ammunition into the gun with a very audible sound, which transmitted down the barrel at the exact moment that I said "We're not here to bring any harm to you." And the Arab looked at me, raised one eyebrow and said, "Oh, really?" This was clearly as bad as it was going to get, and we were very, very close to having to shoot some people to move out of the way. So I gave him my best santa [phoen] salute and I said, "We are both soldiers. If you will not shake my hand, then I will salute you as a fighting man." And I turned to move my vehicles out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At this point in time, Major Kent-Payne, approximately how many soldiers had gathered around -- how many ABiH soldiers or foreign soldiers had gathered around your Warriors?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: I would say minimum 100 and maximum 150. It was -- it was very difficult to count exactly, as it was quite a confined area, but it was around 100 or so local militia and perhaps a maximum of 50 foreigners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, prior to this patrol up the Bila River -- or up the Bila Valley, can you tell the Trial Chamber what type of briefings you had received concerning foreign fighters being in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing whatsoever, then. We were not briefed that they even existed, which was why it came as such a surprise to -- to hear not just the man from Yorkshire but to see Arab soldiers and coloured soldiers there, because we'd had no indication that there was any -- any group of foreign fighters operating in Bosnia at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, after this event on the 15th of May, towards the end of May 1993, what changes, if any, did you notice on the ground in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: When we first arrived in Bosnia, we were briefed by the Cheshire Regiment on the situation. And in the classic way that the British always support the underdog, we were very much of the belief that the BiH, the Bosnian Muslims, were the -- were the underdogs. And this was borne out by the fact that soon after I arrived I helped to -- to remove some bodies from Ahmici and from the massacre, which I'm sure you are aware of, and the fact that at the various checkpoints we went to the BiH soldiers were friendly and courteous and the HVO Croat soldiers were surly and aggressive and clearly saw the United Nations as -- as a barrier to their further expansion. So for the first part of our tour, our first few weeks, we were very much of the impression that the BiH were on the backfoot, that they were on the defensive, and that the bad people, if there was such a thing, were the HVO and the Croats. Towards the end of May, early June, this began to change, and the attitude of the Croats became noticeably softer. They became more cooperative, and they began to hint at the fact that there was a BiH offensive being planned and that they wanted us to assist with their protection. They were clearly worried. And they -- and their attitude towards us became much more compliant. They would let us through checkpoints, and they became more friendly towards us. On the other hand, the BiH attitude became more uncompromising. We had more trouble at BiH checkpoints. And they began to try to prevent us from going into more and more areas that we'd previously had unlimited access to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, you've told us a little bit about patrols and about the policy with respect to not seeking written authorisation. What was the policy, if any, about prior notification to the parties about patrols or missions or where you were going?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: This again was directed to us that we would not give the local -- the local militias any prior indication of our activities. And the reason for this was that to go to a headquarters and basically ask permission to go into a certain area was to admit that the locals controlled Central Bosnia and not the United Nations, which went against the agreement for free passage, then. And indeed, if the -- if such passage was refused, then we would be in a position of basically upping the ante, of being becoming more aggressive by trying to force our way through a particular area in order to complete our mission. So it was the general policy that we did not seek permission to go into any areas because we didn't need to, due to the agreements that had been made between the UN High Command and the high command of the various militias.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you told us a few moments ago that towards the end of May or early June the Croats began to hint at the fact that there was a BiH offensive being planned. What steps, if any, did you take to ascertain whether or not such an offencive was planned -- offensive was planned.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: I had been visiting a village called Grahovcici - again, please excuse the pronunciation - which was a Croat village to the -- to the east of Han Bila then, which was basically a Croat enclave surrounded on three sides by Muslim villages. When we first visited the village, they were quite aggressive and did not want us to enter. And the second time, we were shown into the schoolhouse to meet with the local commander. The third time I visited, I was treated like a long-lost brother by him and I said that I would get one of our officers to come and assess his village for the distribution of UN food aid. And the fourth time, the local commander was clearly very worried and he said to me that he had been told by some of the -- the Muslim inhabitants of the surrounding villages that there was going to be an attack and that him and his family should flee the area to avoid any bloodshed. I asked him how he could be sure that these people were telling the truth, and he told me that the Muslim and the Croat villages have been next to each other for generations and that just because the people were from a different religion didn't mean to say they were not friends and they would look out for each other. I reported this back to the commanding officer, and he convened a meeting in a place called Guca Gora, which is north-east of Travnik, on about the 2nd of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, if I could briefly interrupt you. This fourth visit to Grahovcici that you've just told us about, what day was that, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: As I recall, it was about the 2nd of June, 2003 -- sorry, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So just for clarification, you then reported this information to your commanding officer, who convened a meeting in Guca Gora on the same day?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: I believe it -- I believe it was the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, then, what day the meeting was to be convened in Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: As I recall, the 2nd or 3rd of June. I -- I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber this meeting.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: I personally did not attend the meeting, but I was at Guca Gora that day and I provided the security for the meeting and carried the Croat commanders from -- from Vitez into Guca Gora. The reason we carried them inside our vehicles was because it necessitated them travelling through BiH-held areas and they were worried about their security. So I carried them in my vehicles to this meeting. At one of the intervals, I met some of the -- the delegates, including the Croat commander from Grahovcici, and the deputy commander of 3 Corps BiH, who I knew to be Colonel Merdan, and we discussed -- he spoke a little English. We discussed football, the weather, and then through my interpreter he said that they had agreed there would be no attack and no offensive and I spoke to the Croat commander, and he seemed happy that there would be no attack and that he thanked us for our help in organising it and said he would report back to his people that everything was going to be all right, and the rumours of the attack were just that, rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What happened following this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Following this meeting, we returned back to our camp. And the next day - I believe it was the 3rd of June, 1993 - what we called the lightning offensive, the BiH offensive, took place in the Bila Valley and a number of previously Croat villages were captured by the BiH militia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us that this meeting that you attended in early June 1993 was in Guca Gora. Were there other opportunities or were there other times when you were in the community of Guca Gora in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes. The initial stage of the -- what we knew as the lightning offensive was the capture of villages such as Grahovcici and Brajkovici. But this -- the fighting then spread to the village of Guca Gora. And on about the 7th of June, my company was the guard company and "A" Company under Major Roy Hunter sent a patrol to the area of Guca Gora to monitor the fighting. The reason this was done was because we could hear the fighting from our camp. It was only a few kilometres away, and we did not wish to -- for the same thing to happen as happened in Ahmici, where a massacre took place only a few kilometres from the United Nations base but the United Nations did not know it had happened and, therefore, in the eyes of the International Community did nothing about it. So we had a policy to investigate every -- every burning house, every incident of firing, which was why there was a patrol in Guca Gora. The patrol commander there was fired on by people who were identified as being foreigners. When I say he identified them the site used for the gunnery on the Warrior has a magnification of ten times. And so although a soldier may be 500 metres away and indistinct to the human eye, through the sights it's easily enough to pick up whether he's white-skinned, black-skinned, and of what origin he comes from. They returned fire from the grounds of the monastery in Guca Gora and then herded together the inhabitants of the village to protect them from the attack which was taking place on the village. I was tasked to take a convoy of lorries to the village on the 7th of June to evacuate the civilians. However, when we got to a BiH checkpoint on the Travnik road to turn onto the road through the village of Mosunj and then to Guca Gora, we were blocked by the militia, who said that we could not pass and they had anti-tank mines laid across the road. Also, on the radio we could hear the -- the results of the -- the action taking place in Guca Gora. And as live ammunition was being fired and casualties were being inflicted on the BiH soldiers, it was clearly no place to take soft-skinned lorries. So we were ordered to turn around and we went back to Vitez school. The next morning the commanding officer went to Guca Gora with the UN representative and he instructed that I was to get together as many armoured vehicles as I could, and we got together 16 assorted armoured vehicles and drove to the checkpoint on the road to Travnik. The mines were still there and the BiH soldiers refused to let us through, saying that we could not go into a security zone. I told them that we already had soldiers in Guca Gora and they said they would let them out but not me in and that they would refuse to let any Croats out in our vehicles. I then asked them to move the mines again, and they refused. So we got our vehicle and by very carefully moving from left to right with the tracks on the smooth tarmac we pushed the anti-tank mines out of the way, which was risky and rather stupid, but the only way to get through this particular checkpoint. And the BiH decided that we clearly wanted to carry out our task, so they let us through. Once we got to Guca Gora, there were a large number of Croat civilians, 181, to be precise, and we succeeded in fitting them into our vehicles, which we then turned round to head back down to -- to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, to the best of your recollection, what time was it when you arrived at the monastery in Guca Gora on that day?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: It was late morning, probably 11.00 in the morning, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately how long did it take to load the 181 civilians into the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: It took -- it took about two hours, simply because we could only load one vehicle at a time, because there was shooting taking place at this stage. The civilians were in safe cover inside the monastery. But we had one vehicle at a time parked in front of the monastery in a place where there was a large wall and could not be seen from much of the village, and it was a safe place to put these people in. Also, we knew we had to pack at least 10 or 15 people into each vehicle to ensure that they were inside armoured protection, and this took some time to pack them in. We also moved the children and the women first, and then followed by old men and finally men of combatant age. And this took some time to sort them out as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than the 181 civilians, was anything else taken from the monastery in Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: The -- the abbot in charge of the monastery asked our regimental padre, that's our -- our spiritual advisor, then, who is a commissioned officer, whether he would be willing to assist in moving some of the religious artifacts from the monastery into safekeeping. And he suggested that the -- the main church in Vitez would be a good place to take these items. I said that we would not be able to take very much, and I asked him why it was important. And he told me that it was a very, very old monastery and an important religious site for the Croat -- for the Roman Catholic religion. We took some statues, some other artifacts, and the leather-bound Bible from the altar. The Abbott took me up to the library there, where there were several thousand books, and it was clearly impossible to take very many of these books. And finally, then, the Abbott and our padre locked the door and we left and he was the last person into the vehicles. And when we evacuated, there were no Croats left alive in -- in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber the condition of the monastery on the 8th of June, 1993 when you left, when you locked the door and departed.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: I was inside the monastery building for approximately half an hour as we briefed the local people T Croats as to what was going to happen. We told them how the evacuation would be conducted, and we got them into the order which we wished to take them out to the vehicles. As I recall, the monastery was extremely old. It had a large number of wooden seats, with a wooden confessional box for the priest, and on one wall was a large -- a large painted mural or fresco which struck me as being out of place, as the church was clearly very old, but this mural had probably been painted in the last 20 years and was very abstract and modern. There was no damage to the inside of the church, other than it was untidy, having been the home to almost 200 people for -- for 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, major Kent-Payne.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I'm about to move into a larger area of my direct examination, and this is approximately the time for the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. We are going to make a break. It's quarter to 4.00. We shall continue at ten past 4.00. This is also going to allow our witness to take some rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, right before we took a recess, you were describing for us the evacuation of a number of civilians from Guca Gora. Did you on any subsequent occasion return to the monastery at Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes. About five days later, I was tasked by the United Nations civil advisor to the commanding officer, whose name was Randy Rhodes, to go to the village of Maljine, which is about 2 or 3 kilometres from Guca Gora. The -- one of the liaison officers, Captain Mark Bower, had been given a map which -- by a Croat which was supposed to show the site of an atrocity which had been committed by BiH or foreign soldiers in Maljine, and the map showed where the bodies were buried. And this -- the permission to go to -- go to this area was sought and given, and so on about the 13th of June, 1993, I took around six or eight armoured vehicles up to Guca Gora with the aim of taking Randy Rhodes and Mark Bower to the village of Maljine to search for any signs of the supposed atrocity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, again approximately what time on 13 June 1993 did you leave the Vitez school where you were garrisoned?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Again, we would have left at about 9.00 in the morning and got to Guca Gora about 9.45, 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, what happened as your convoy approached Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: As we arrived in Guca Gora, it was immediately apparent that there were a large number of heavily armed men in and around the monastery. We were stopped by people standing in front of us outside the monastery, and I noticed a large number of foreigners, people who we now knew to be known as the Mujahedin in the area of the monastery. There were or there was a heavy machine-gun in a sandbagged emplacement outside the monastery and approximately 20 to 30 foreign soldiers and about 10 to 15 locals, mostly middle-aged men from the local BiH militia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you on that occasion have any interaction with any of the people who were standing in front of you on the road?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes. At first, I dismounted and went forward to what was a small checkpoint across the road, and I was then confronted by a foreigner who I had not seen before, again, of North African appearance, who spoke a little English. And I said my mission was to go to Maljine and that I had to search the area and it will be better for his side if he allowed us to go there because it would show that they had nothing to hide. He refused this request and said that we must turn back. And in the vehicle with me I also had some press with them. They got out of the vehicle and started to film, and this made the foreigners extremely agitated at the prospect of appearing on the camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what type of clothing these individuals were wearing.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Again, a mixture of uniform and civilian dress. But in -- and a number of them had -- had Arabic headdress, what we call in the British Army Shemagues, a chequered red-and-white headdress which wraps around their head. Some of them had what I would describe as afghan outfits, their baggy trouser, waistcoats, almost turban-like head gear. And quite a few had long beards, including some with henna in the beards. But all wore -- all wore some form of military fatigues, either trousers or jackets, to -- to make people know that they were -- they were in some form of military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Major, when I interrupted you you were telling us about the press beginning to photograph these people with cameras. Can you please continue.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: The -- the foreigners got most agitated at this and to diffuse the situation I told the -- the film cameraman to get back inside the vehicle and I tasked one of my soldiers to ensure that he did not go outside the vehicle again.
