The -- the fighters who were present did not seem unduly upset by the -- the two written reporters from the newspapers, and they continued to -- to write down what was going then on at this time. At one stage when I went back to my vehicle and stood in the turret to brief my vehicle gunner as to what was happening and to what procedure to follow, I was level with the bank of grass outside the monastery and one man spoke to me in a heavily Yorkshire accented English, basically telling me to go home. And I said to him, "I think we come from the same place. Why don't you go home too." And he then -- he then started swearing at me. And I said, "Look, we're all Yorkshire brothers." And he said, "You're definitely not my brother," and then started to insult British and UNPROFOR in general. About a minute later, just as I was about to dismount from the vehicle, one of the local militia there, a middle-aged man in his late 50s, early 60s then accidentally fired his rifle into the ground at his feet. Then my soldiers in the vehicles took this to be a form of aggression and we swung the turrets of our vehicles on to the foreigners on the bank around the monastery and we loaded our weapons with both -- both high explosive and machine-gun ammunition. At this point the British member of the Mujahedin shouted to everyone to cool down, to calm down, which -- which most people did. And eventually the situation calmed down again. I moved forward to the checkpoint and talked again to the -- to the man of North African origin. And a few minutes later a white Toyota pick-up arrived and out of it got the same Arab who I'd met at Fazlici about three weeks before. He walked up to me. He clearly didn't recognise me. The first time I'd met him had been -- I'd been wearing my helmet. This time I was wearing a beret. And I'd started to grow a moustache, so I probably looked slightly different. I recognised him though and I deliberately held out my hand to shake hands with him, and he again said, "I will not shake the hand of an infidel." I knew then it was the same man. He again said too me, "I will not talk with a woman present." And it was a different female interpreter, and I sent her back to the vehicle. Myself and Randy Rhodes and Mark Bower talked to this man for 15 to 20 minutes. And again it became clear that he was not going to let us go to Maljine and he kept on telling us that the problem he had with this was that he would not let our vehicles into what he called his security zone. I then said to him, "If it's -- if it's my vehicles you object to, will you let me go to the village unarmed and with my colleagues here?" And this put him on the defensive. And he had no choice really but to agree to that. So he summons the pick-up truck back to him, and myself and Mark and Randy got into this. The only weapons we had were our pistols, which were under our flak jackets. The vehicle -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Major. At the -- at the time you got into the pick-up truck, approximately what time was it?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: I would say about 10.45, 11.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And prior to getting into the pick-up truck, what orders, if any, did you give to your unit or your soldiers who remained with the warriors at this checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: I had a slightly bad feeling about this, because we were going way outside the mandate of what we were supposed to do; although, to my opinion, the primary task was to get to this village, to investigate the alleged atrocity. So I briefed my company second-in-command that we would be gone for one hour and if we were not back in one hour and he had not heard from us, then we were -- then he was to force the checkpoint and take as many vehicles as possible to -- to Maljine and look for me. I also gave -- gave him my signet ring to give to my girlfriend if something bad happened to me. We then got into the pick-up truck and the driver set off in reverse gear and drove straight into a lamppost, which lightened up the atmosphere somewhat, and we had a good laugh about this as we set off. As we drove down the roads to Maljine, I noticed a number of Arabic slogans painted on the walls of buildings. And every time we passed groups of people the Arab leader would shake his fist out the leader and shout "Allah-U-Ekber." And the same cry was returned by the peoples there. And this was not something we had seen before. As to us it represented both fundamentalism -- and also they were not speaking in Serbo-Croat but in Arabic, which was a different -- a different situation and interpretation to what we'd been used to. We spent about 35 to 40 minutes in Maljine. The -- we did not go off the -- off the hard surfaces for fear of antipersonnel mines there, so we went from the roads to the buildings and back onto the roads again. In two or three of the buildings there were -- there were bloodstains on the floor, and outside there were several dead pigs and also dogs, which we assumed had been shot by the foreigners. Then we saw no signs of any atrocities. It was impossible to tell whether the blood was human or animal there. It soon became clear that the map which Captain Bower had was absolutely useless and it had no scale on it, no north pointer on it, and it was impossible to -- to make it fit any of the recognisable features in the village. So frankly, we went through the motions for, I'd say, 35 to 40 minutes, and then asked to be taken back to our vehicles, as I wanted to ensure that I was back well within the hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, Major Kent-Payne, approximately what time you then returned to the checkpoint where you had left your Warriors and the remaining members of "C" Company?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Without going back in my statement, it would -- it would have been one hour after we -- after we left, because I ensured that we were back one hour after we left so that my -- so that my troops, who remained at Guca Gora, were not put in the position of having to carry out my orders of forcing through the checkpoint to come to our aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After returning to that checkpoint, what did you and the remaining soldiers in "C" Company do? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: I spoke to -- to Randy Rhodes, who was upset with us and said that we'd taken too many risks to fulfil our task. And I told him that -- that it was him that gave us the job in the first place and if he didn't really want us to do it, then why did he give us the job. And he calmed down at that. We then -- we then thanked the -- the local commander for his cooperation, and I told him that the -- the press would report what we had seen and it would probably show the -- the BiH in a good light. And then we received permission to move our vehicles into the village square, and we turned round and headed back the way we came, back to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Prior to the recess, sir, you told us about the attack on the area, including Grahovcici. At any point after that attack in early June, did you return to the village of Grahovcici?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes. The next day, which as I recall was the 14th of June, then, I was tasked by the -- by the battalion operations officer to pick up a United Nations field worker and take him to -- to Grahovcici, where there had been a report that another atrocity had been committed. By "atrocity" I mean that local people had been killed by the attacking BiH soldiers or that Croat soldiers who had surrendered or had been captured had been executed then. So at about five past 9.00 in the morning, I picked up the United Nations field worker and also a number of members of the media, including a film crew and a newspaper reporter. And we headed first of all to -- to Zenica, and then across the road that leads through Cajdras, Novo Selo, and then to Grahovcici. The reason we did not head up the -- the Bila Valley to Han Bila was that the Croats, fearing for a BiH push down the Bila Valley towards Nova Bila had fortified their checkpoint and were not keen on letting us through into this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, was there any particular reason why you went to Zenica on that morning?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: No. When I say -- when I say "Zenica," we actually went -- we bypassed Zenica on what we called the mountain road to get to -- get to Cajdras checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many vehicles and how many men went on this mission?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Again, this was two Warrior, with approximately 10 soldiers, a female interpreter, and some four members of the -- of the media, a film cameraman and two or three -- two or three news reporters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Chamber what happened as you made your way towards Grahovcici on the morning of 14 June 1993.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: We were stopped at the Cajdras road junction by -- at a BiH checkpoint. There was a -- a log across the road, and I dismounted to talk to the soldiers to ask them to move it out of the way. The first thing I noticed about them was how well dressed they were, and they were actually wearing -- wearing dark -- dark brown berets with a small cap badge with the BiH -- BiH logo on it. And we had a pleasant conversation, but they said that they would not let me through their checkpoint without papers from the corps commander. I gave them the normal story, that we would not be able to do this, and they said in that case we could not go through the -- go through the checkpoint. At the time we arrived at the checkpoint, it was about 9.45 in the morning, and by about 10.30 the BiH soldiers had reinforced the checkpoint with land mines to put on the road and deployed a heavy machine-gun to emphasise the point they did not want us to go through. Again, it was clearly obvious that they weren't going to let us through, so I decided to call their bluff and as this -- as the UN aid worker was saying that this was a very, very important task, I decided to go to 3 Corps headquarters in Zenica and see if I could obtain one of these mysterious pieces of paper to actually see if it would work. We turned around, and I left one vehicle at the checkpoint and with the other Warrior we drove to 3 Corps headquarters, which was in a -- a requisitioned factory complex in Zenica. At the -- at the gate there, I said to the soldier in charge that I wanted to see the corps commander. And he made a telephone call, and a young staff officer appeared and took myself and the interpreter upstairs to an office where I was shown in to the office of Colonel Merdan, the deputy corps commander. I told him about the checkpoint, and he -- he said that we should have been let through. And we talked for 10 or 15 minutes. And I said, "Look, I need this piece of paper from the corps commander if I'm to complete my task." He then showed me through the -- through his office into the corps commander's office, where I met General Hadzihasanovic for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, if I could briefly interrupt you at this point. My first question is: Approximately what time was it when you arrived at either the office of Colonel Merdan or the time approximately when you were taken into General Hadzihasanovic's office?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: We spent 45 minutes at the checkpoint. We left there around 10.30 in the morning and arrived at the corps headquarters maybe 15 minutes later. So it would have been about 11.00, 11.15 by the time we were shown into the general's office. I have a clear recollection of the timings because -- because as things transpired later in the day, the timings became quite important as to -- as to how long we were delayed. And I -- I asked people how long we'd spent at each location, which was -- which is why I'm reasonably specific about how long the various events of this particular day took.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also told us that this was the first time you met General Hadzihasanovic. Do you know or do you recall approximately how many times after this day you saw or spoke to General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: I met the general only three, four times. The first three or four times were in his headquarters, and I believe he came to a meeting in the officer's mess at Vitez as well. And I met him semi-socially then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On this day, that is, 14 June 1993, approximately how long were you in General Hadzihasanovic's office?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: I would say for about 30 minutes, during which time I introduced myself. I told him a little bit about my background. He told me a little bit about his background. And I -- I commented that it was strange how only -- only the corps commander could give permission for me to pass through one particular checkpoint. And I said, "In my army, this would be done by a very junior officer." And he said words to the effect of, "You have to remember that we're a very young army and it takes a long time for us to get rid of the old controlling ways of the Yugoslav National Army. And when there is peace, then we'll have time to transform ourselves into -- into a more westernised army, like you come from." And I understood his problems then, that he was the only person who could make this particular decision to allow me through this checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the approximately 30 minutes that you were in General Hadzihasanovic's office, did you notice items that were in his office?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: It was as I expected a senior officer's office to be. There were -- there were maps on his desk and a couple of maps on the wall, then. Again, I couldn't resist being nosey, so I was looking over his shoulder to see what the maps were with the intention of perhaps gleaning some low-level information to pass back to our military information cell back in Vitez. There was a map of the Bila Valley then with large arrows on it, which is exactly the same as we would have in our headquarters for an operational planning map, to show the -- the big picture of any military operation and then the more junior commanders would then have more detailed maps based off this. It was exactly as I would have expected a general's office to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told the Trial Chamber that you went to this office to receive a pass to get through the checkpoint. Did you in fact receive such a pass?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: No. The general said that it was -- it was ridiculous for us to have a piece of paper for this and that he would go even better than that and he would provide us with a -- a BiH military policeman, who would ensure that we got through not just the Cajdras checkpoint but through any other checkpoints we encountered on the way to Grahovcici. And I got the impression that he was ensuring that if -- if the piece of paper was taken off us by one particular checkpoint, then we would still be able to continue with the -- with the military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, then, Major, in -- at this point in time, on the morning of the 14th of June, 1993, you did not receive such a pass; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Absolutely. By this time, it was about 11.30 in the morning. And the general asked us to wait in an -- in an anteroom, where we went and sat and had some tea or coffee, then. And I expected that the military policeman would arrive soon afterwards. In fact, it was well over an hour, an hour and 15 minutes before someone finally told us that the car with the military policeman was waiting outside. By this time it must have been 12.30, 1.00, and we followed the military policeman in a Lada police car to the Cajdras checkpoint, where he got out and talked to the militiamen for about five minutes, during which time it was clear that they were not happy that we'd actually fulfilled our promise to go back to the corps headquarters but they had no choice but to let us through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did your convoy consisting of the two Warriors and the BiH military police car then proceed towards Grahovcici?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we went along the road. There were another couple of small checkpoints, which the military policeman successfully negotiated us through, until we arrived at another checkpoint in a village called Novo Selo. Here we were stopped by more soldiers with a makeshift barricade across the road, and they then started to have a heated argument with the military policeman. I went forward to see what was happening and was told that, first of all, that the -- they accused the military policeman of being a Croat spy. And I said, "Is it likely that I'll be escorting a Croat spy in a BiH military police car?" But they said, "We don't know this man. He could be anyone. And anyway, we need a piece of paper from the corps commander to come through."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, if I could again interrupt. The people at the checkpoint in Novo Selo, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Again, a mixture of -- of fatigue uniforms, and there were a number of militiamen there who were wearing Arabic-type headdress. However, from their facial appearance, it was clear that they were -- they were Bosnians. We had amongst ourselves, the British soldiers, we classified the -- the BiH soldiers into a number of categories. At the -- at the top end, as the most serious and most dangerous, were the foreign Mujahedin, the Arabic fighters, if you like; at the bottom end, the easiest to deal with were the local militia, often middle-aged men, who were just only interested in basically getting home in one piece at the end of the day; and next up from that were the regular units of the BiH, who were normally reasonably easily to deal with; and then there was an organisation called 7 Muslim Brigade. These consisted of the more hard line of the BiH soldiers. By that I mean the more -- the people with the stricter adherence to the Muslim faith. Then a lot of them affected long beards, some items of Arabic and Afghan-type dress, then. And a number of these went, as far as they could, to be like the foreign Mujahedin. And we called these plastic Mujahedin, plastic being a derogatory term for imitation. And so they pretended to be Arabs with long beards and Arabic headdress but they weren't the real thing; they were actually Bosnians. And there were five or six of these individuals there, and they were by far the most aggressive of the soldiers at this particular checkpoint. And the others were normal Bosnian soldiers from 7 Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based, Major Payne, on your experience and the information that you possessed at the time when you encountered these soldiers at the checkpoint in Novo Selo, did you know what unit they were affiliated with?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Absolutely, because I asked them. They -- I said, "Look, look, you've already let me through your checkpoint at Cajdras and you've already -- and why won't you let the military policeman through now?" And they said, "That's because we're a different brigade." And I said, "Okay, which brigade are you then?" And they said, "We're from --" they called it 7 Mountain Brigade, in fact, there. And I said, "What do I need to get through your checkpoint?" And they said, "We need a piece of paper signed by the corps commander." And we talked about this for 10 or 15 minutes. And then I said to them, "Okay, I'm going to get this piece of paper now and you'll be in trouble when I get back and you'll see that I get this." And they looked at me as if to say there's no way you're going to achieve this -- this mission.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would be grateful for a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, I assume you heard what the interpreter just said. Did you then in fact make an attempt to get such a piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes. We turned round again and with our military policeman we returned to 3 Corps headquarters in Zenica. I went up to see Colonel Merdan again, and he said that we were to wait and that the general would eventually sign the piece of paper that we needed. I asked to see General Hadzihasanovic because I wanted to tell him myself the trouble we were having going about our legitimate business as part of the United Nations. So I saw the general for about five -- five minutes, and he said yes, he would definitely arrange the piece of paper for us. I assumed that he would sign it there and then and give it to me, but this was Bosnia and things didn't happen that way, so we were shown outside to an anteroom and I remember we were given a glass of vodka to drink, which was unusual, because we normally were given slivovice in various headquarters. And we waited and we waited for approximately 1 hour and 15 minutes before we were finally given the piece of paper at about half past 4.00, 5.00 in the afternoon. The piece of paper was -- had been written on a typewriter with the -- the general's name and a signature above this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major, armed with this piece of paper, what did you then do?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: I took the piece of paper, went back to the vehicles, and then we drove back to -- to Novo Selo. And where I showed it to the -- the commander of the checkpoint, who looked most upset that we'd gone to the trouble to get it but it was clearly -- it was clearly the correct item. He recognised the signature, the name, the -- the crest on the piece of paper, and had no option but to let us through. We were only about 1 kilometre from Grahovcici, and by this stage it was about half past 6.00, perhaps even 7.00 at night. And it was starting to get dark. The UN aid worker then came to me and said that he was only contracted to work until 5.00 and would we -- would we come back another day. My reply to him was unprintable, but I pointed out that he had asked me to go to the village in the first place and we were going to continue with our task, as we'd been at it for about eight or nine hours at this stage to get our way to Grahovcici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major, approximately how far was Grahovcici from your garrison in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Without looking at the map, I can't be sure, but no more than 6 or 7 kilometres. But its location meant it was in the hills above us, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And under normal conditions, how long would it take for two Warriors to travel from Vitez to Grahovcici?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: The particular route that we took should have taken from -- from the Cajdras checkpoint to Grahovcici should have taken about 20, 25 minutes. But obviously it took us several hours to complete this journey with the various delays and waits at 3 Corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So I believe you've told us, sir, that it was sometime between 18.30 and 19.00 on the 14th of June, 1993 when you finally arrived at Grahovcici?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: So from first arriving at the Cajdras checkpoint at about 10.00 in the morning, it had taken us almost nine hours to fulfil this particular task and actually get our vehicles, and more importantly, the UN observer to the -- to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what in fact happened once you delivered the UN worker to Grahovcici?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: As I said, it was getting dusk at this point, so we -- we didn't have that long, probably 40, 50 minutes in the village. We walked around. There were several dead pigs and dogs lying around, some bloodstains, but no bodies and no obvious sign that there had been an atrocity, no freshly-turned earth or anything like that. As an infantry soldier, I had a look around the defensive positions from the Croats, and there had clearly been a heavy battle for this village. There were several hundred, if not thousand, empty cases in and around the trenches. The marks of -- where mortar bombs had exploded and other discarded ordnance from that. There were no -- no civilians there. There were no -- or very few signs of any BiH soldiers. And from what I could see, none of the buildings had been -- had been burned or destroyed in any other way, other than through normal battle damage. After about 50 minutes the UN worker virtually plead to be taken away and we had clearly done what we were asked to do, so we drove him back to Vitez, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, do you recall the next time that you went to the area of Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes. What -- what happened was the -- the checkpoints that the BiH had put up in the area of Guca Gora were removed around the 14th, 15th of -- of June. And the reason for this was that we had been asked by the HVO, the Croat militia, to go to the village of Pokrajcici, which is to the west of the Bila Valley, then, to take part in a body exchange. We'd done this and helped to recover the bodies of some HVO soldiers from the front line. And in return for this favour, I'd ask the local Croat commander for vehicles of my company to be allowed to drive along his front line. What this effectively meant was that we could get from Vitez to Guca Gora without having to go through any BiH checkpoints. So there was clearly no point in putting them there, because they couldn't stop us from getting into the area any more. So on the 16th of June, I took a patrol along the Croat front line and -- to Guca Gora with a task of assessing whether the foreigners were still encamped around the monastery and to what the situation was, whether they'd burned the village or anything else. We arrived at the -- the monastery and stopped outside. And as I took my radio headset off, I could hear the sound of broken glass inside the monastery. And I got out of my vehicle, and with an interpreter and my bodyguard went forward to the door and pushed it open. Inside the monastery were 20 or 30 women, mostly middle-aged and elderly, who were sweeping up the monastery and cleaning it, and the sound that I'd heard had been broken glass being swept up and then put into -- into buckets there. In addition to sweeping the floor, they had cloths with water and they were wiping the walls down and trying to remove the Arabic slogans which had been painted on the walls. I looked around me, and it was clear there was a considerable amount of -- of damage or desecration had been done to the inside of the monastery. As I recall, the -- the wooden confessional booth had been smashed up and burned, several of the wooden seats had been smashed, and there was human excrement smeared on the rest there. There had been pots of paint thrown at the -- the large fresco on the wall and Arabic slogans had been written on the -- on the walls in spray-paint. And finally, an attempt had been made to hack the -- the fresco from the wall with something like a pickaxe or a shovel and there were large pieces of plaster and dirt on the floor where this had happened. It was clear -- it was clear to me is that there had been a substantial amount of desecration of this -- this particular religious building and a few minutes later a BiH policeman appeared and said that we had to remove from the area immediately. And I told him words to the effect of, "In America they call this a cover-up, but I've seen what you're doing and I will report it." And he told me that he had been instructed by 3 Corps headquarters in Zenica to do as much as he could with these women to make good the damage that had been done to the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, were there any future dates or days when you were at the monastery in Guca Gora, after this event you've told us about on the 16th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: At the end of the month of June 1993, about the 30th of June, I was tasked by the operations officer to take the -- the priest from the church in Vitez, together with our own padre, to the monastery in Guca Gora. Like many things in Bosnia, rumours were rife and the Croats believed that the Bosnian Muslims had completely destroyed the monastery and they'd burnt it down, and the object of taking the priest there was to show him the damage that had been done but so he could go back to reassure his people that actually the building had not been razed to the ground, as many people believed. In order to do this, I was instructed to go to 3 Corps headquarters and obtain written permission from the corps headquarters to get me through any checkpoints which I would need to pass through to get to Guca Gora, and also to give to the military policeman there, to give him written authority to show us around the monastery. At 3 Corps headquarters, I did not see the general but I -- I met up with the deputy corps commander, Colonel Merdan. And I said to him that the desecration of the monastery was a very serious act and that we heard many, many times that it was only the HVO, or the Croats and the Serbs who destroyed religious sites - for instance, the mosques in Ahmici and Bandol were completely destroyed by the HVO - and I told him that by allowing their own people to desecrate the monastery in Guca Gora, as far as the International Community would be concerned they were making themselves as bad as the other two sides and that the HVO, the Croats, would clearly use this as propaganda to say that the -- the BiH were committing the same form of -- of desecration. Colonel Merdan said to me that it was not regular troops that is did this, but it was the foreigners, the Mujahedin. And I said to him words to the effect of, "But they're under your control and therefore you are responsible for doing this." And he said an analogy on the lines of, "But you have to understand that -- that the foreigners are like the -- the genie in Aladdin, then. You can rub the lamp and get the genie out to help you. But unlike the genie who returns to the lamp, then the foreigners are very difficult to get back into their box and they're difficult to control." And he said that it's -- it was something that they needed to -- to work on, to ensure that these people did not behave in a manner which -- which was -- which was unbecoming and which was against the Geneva Convention. We went from there to the monastery, and indeed a very good effort had been made to clean up the place there. The slogans had been removed from the walls. The -- the place had been tidied up and swept clean. But you can't -- you can't unsmash a 500--year-old window and they couldn't obviously repair the fresco, so that damage had still been done. And that was the last time for several weeks that I went to Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major, when Colonel Merdan made this statement about Aladdin and the genie, what was your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: I believed that he was acknowledging the fact that the foreigners were part of his organisation but they were clearly an undisciplined part of his organisation and something that he was wishing to control but perhaps wasn't sure how best to do it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In terms of the information that you received and things that you observed while on the ground in Bosnia, what conclusions, if any, did you draw about the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: They were quite clearly -- quite clearly fanatical and saw both the HVO and indeed the United Nations as the enemy. From the evidence that I saw around Guca Gora and from anecdotal evidence from other UN commanders, I believe that the foreigners were used to spearhead any attack by 3rd Corps BiH and that they formed part of what we knew as 7 Muslim Brigade, which was also used as the fire brigade, if you like, for 3 Corps. And it -- it was clear to me that they were perhaps indisciplined and out of control but nevertheless were acting as part of the organisation that we knew as 3 Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you explain for the Trial Chamber what you mean by "spearhead."

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes. In any -- in any attack, it needs someone to form the very front line of that attack, and this was often carried out by the foreigners from 7 Brigade, with the 7 Brigade troops behind them. There were a number of reasons for this, I believe, as a soldier, then: First of all, the foreigners were the best equipped and perhaps the more fanatical fighters; then secondly, they were foreigners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Stop, please. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the questions put by my learned friend at the moment are calling for the opinion on behalf of the witness about the facts that he cannot testify to and that he has not testified about today. The opinions are something that we have mentioned on several occasions from the beginning of this trial. We are trying to allow our learned friend to examine in any way he wants; however, during our cross-examination, we are going to try and establish the base for the opinion that the witness is asked to put forward. We are here on very slippery ground at the moment because the witness is being asked to talk about his military knowledge. Usually these are the questions that are put to experts. This witness is not an expert. If he is, he has not been defined as an expert. He was on the ground. But if my learned friend wants to ask him questions about who was leading the attacks, then he -- the witness has to either tell us that he saw the attacks or that he received data of some units spearheading these attacks. The witness has spoken about very precise incidents, an incident at the checkpoint, an incident by the monastery in Guca Gora, and another incident when he went to Grahovcici village to inspect the area. On no occasion did he mention any other attacks, unless we take into consideration the thing -- the fact that he saw a map in the general's office with the arrows on the map. I don't think it is proper for us to talk about who was it who carried out an attack, who was in command, only if one is a soldier on the ground. Mr. President, if we allow this witness to testify in this way, then we will have to apply the same thing to all the other witnesses. And if all the witnesses are to testify in this way, we are going to go far from the evidence that you are supposed to hear that might be useful to you to arrive at the truth about this case. I believe that we have already mentioned the difference between expert witnesses and opinions put forth by any other witness. For that reason, Mr. President, the Defence would like the Chamber to rule about opinions put forth by witnesses. And we will act upon your oral ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we render our decision, what is the viewpoint of the Prosecution? Let me summarise. The Prosecution has called for an opinion on the part of the witness in their question. The question was what the Mujahedin did. And the witness said that they spearheaded all of the attacks. The Prosecution then asked the witness to define the term "spearheading." And then he answered that in every army there are parts of the troops who form the very front line of the attack and that in this particular case those were foreigners, the Mujahedin. Mr. Mundis, with regard to --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just add something to what Mr. Bourgon has said, before the Prosecution responds.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: And that is that we do support the submission that has been made by Mr. Bourgon. The witness, his evidence should be limited to what he saw and experienced and knew at the time. Your Honours have already ruled in relation to previous witnesses, that they should only be allowed to testify about relevant matters in the case and in particular, about what they knew or saw at the time. And we -- we would respectfully submit that in this case it's imperative that the witness's testimony is limited to what he himself is able to testify about and not allow the witness to make extrapolations or assumptions. Those are matters, of course, for Your Honours to consider in due course, and the parties will be able to address Your Honours on those questions as well. Your Honour, the main reason for that, in our submission, is that the probative value that can be attached to opinions or assumptions that the -- the witness makes is very limited, and there must be circumstances, in our submission where, because the probative value that can potentially be attached is of such a narrow value that it should be excluded, that Your Honours should not allow such evidence to be put before Your Honours, to be put in public session, because of the potential prejudicial effect to the accused. In your submission, the trial cannot be run on the basis of rumours and assumptions; it must be based on hard facts. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mundis. What is the position of the Prosecution with regard to the observations put forth by the Defence? Mr. Dixon has just added that those who form the very front line of the attack is something that the witness only heard from other people, that he cannot testify directly about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution would respectfully request that the witness be removed from the courtroom in order for us to fully respond to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm going to ask the usher to take the witness out of the room for a while. Witness, you are going to leave the courtroom for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First, for the record, again the Prosecution was asking the witness about any conclusions that he reached based on information he had received and things that he had observed. As the Defence is well aware and as has been repeatedly litigated in this case, hearsay evidence is admissible, assuming that the source of that hearsay information is known to the Chamber. So with respect to the hearsay component, the Prosecution would assert that there is absolutely no reason why a witness couldn't draw conclusions based on hearsay, just as he could draw conclusions based on any other information that's in that witness's possession. The witness has testified about several events from which one could conclude or one might reasonably conclude that there was a degree of interaction between the foreign fighters and members of the ABiH, including some of the incidents at the checkpoints. With respect to the question about spearheading, simply that goes again to demonstrate that information that was in the witness's possession from briefings he received or from intelligence report s that he might have received led him to certain conclusions. He's clearly not testifying as a expert witness, we have not called him as an expert witness, and the Defence know that is we have not called him as an expert witness. There have been a number of witnesses, however, whom the Prosecution have asked about conclusions they reached based on things they observed or information that was in their possession. The Prosecution would assert that this is clearly a proper line of questioning. Mr. Dixon is certainly correct that it's a question of weight to be given to such evidence. The Prosecution would submit, however, that it's certainly not rising to the level of being prejudicial or unfairly prejudicial to the accused simply because we're here before an International Tribunal of professional Judges who can assess this evidence and give it the proper weight. The issue of weight to be given to the evidence, when Your Honours finally have to deliberate on the issues involved in this case, does not in any way go to the admissibility of the evidence. The evidence is certainly in the Prosecution's view admissible. The issue of what weight Your Honours might ultimately give it is a completely different matter, and that is evidence, the weight to be given to this evidence, the Prosecution would submit, is more properly done at the end of the trial, when all the evidence is available to Your Honours. This is particularly the case in cases such as this one that are highly or to a certain -- to a large extent rely on circumstantial evidence. Your Honours clearly are being given small pieces of the puzzle which will only be clear at the end of the case. We would submit that what is involved here at this point is the admissibility of this evidence, not the weight to be given to it. We believe that it clearly is admissible at this point, based on the practice of this Trial Chamber, and also given the fact of what the witness has testified to, the knowledge that he had, the observations that he made, which all went into him reaching these conclusions. Again, Mr. President, I know the Prosecution has raised this on several other occasions, but we would respectfully again request the Defence that in the event they want to raise such objections or any lengthy objections involving submissions by counsel, that they respectfully request the witness to be taken out of the courtroom. The Prosecution does not think it's proper to be arguing before the Chamber in the presence of the witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Before I give the floor to Mr. Bourgon, I have to clarify something. On page 64, line 23 of this discussion, it says -- the Prosecution asked the witness the following: "According to the information that you had and according to what you were able to observe yourself, what did -- what conclusions could you draw about the Mujahedin?" The first element of this question was the information that the witness had; and the second element was what he could observe and what could he conclude about the Mujahedin, based on these two elements. On page 65, line 1, the witness replied that he was of the opinion that the Mujahedins spearheaded the attacks. The next question by the Prosecution was: What do you mean by spearheading the attacks? And the witness then said, "In any attack, there are troops who form the very front line of the attack." And the witness said that those were, in this case, the foreigners in the 7th Brigade. Having said that, I would like to give the floor to the Defence, and then we will retire to deliberate and to decide whether the witness will be allowed to continue answering this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I believe that the Chamber has been able to identify the exact question that we are objecting to. The witness was asked to provide an answer based on two elements: The information that he had received and the observations that he made himself. And then the question was for him to draw conclusions about the Mujahedins. In the witness's answer, we believe that there is a danger in allowing such evidence to be heard. The witness said that the Mujahedin were those that the HVO and the United Nations regarded as the enemy. He never spoke about the HVO and the UN before. He mentioned this for the first time today. Secondly, the Mujahedin treated the UN as the enemy. Today we have spoken about two incidents. In one of them, according to the witness, the United Nations were treated as the hostile force. The tensions rose. And during that same incident, there was a soldier who was involved who happened to fire his weapon. And this resulted in a situation in which the UN troops turned their barrels against the Mujahedin, and then the witness said that he mounted the vehicle and he said that he was then taken to Maljine. He never said that the Mujahedin treated the UN as the enemy. He said that based on what he saw in Guca Gora and the anecdotal evidence from various commanders he concluded some things. What he saw in Guca Gora were some people that he believed were Mujahedin, and he also saw some inscriptions in the Arabic script in the monastery, but he never saw anything that would illustrate the behaviour of these people. If there had indeed been any attacks by the army or the Mujahedin, the witness did not eyewitness any of that. He -- the witness also mentioned a genie in the lamp. He never mentioned who was the one who did the rubbing of the lamp. We may draw our conclusions based on that. What we may conclude is that the 7th Brigade spearheaded the attacks together with the Mujahedin. If the Trial Chamber allows the witness to draw such conclusions without his words being part of the context, without his words being based firmly on the facts, it is our opinion that this may be detrimental. A witness may appear someday who will speak in favour of one side or the other. The witness is supposed to say what he saw, what he witnessed. A lot of things are being allowed here for a witness to say. A fact witness is allowed to put forth his opinions, and this may be detrimental for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will retire to deliberate, but before we do that I would like to give the floor to Mr. Dixon again. Let me tell you that in lines 19 and 20 the witness did put forth an opinion about something that was said by the Mujahedin against the UN. This Mujahedin had a Yorkshire accent and he attacked both the Brits and the UN. Mr. Dixon, you have the floor. Then we will retire.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Only one further point, and that is the witness only mentioned the 7th Brigade on one occasion, when he says he was allegedly stopped by them at a checkpoint for a few minutes. That's the only time the 7th Brigade has been mentioned. The next question concerning the 7th Brigade which arose is the one that we objected to. And our plain submission is -- therein lies the danger of asking these kinds of questions, is that a huge jump has been taken by the witness with no justification, in our submission, because it is based on general assumptions, extrapolations, and not based on what the witness knew or saw. And we would ask Your Honours to consider our objection in light of the evidence that the witness has already given, in particular about the 7th Brigade. Your Honours might well reply that these are questions we could put to the witness in cross-examination. However, in our submission, because of the gap between what the witness has actually said in his testimony and the conclusion that he -- he now draws, we say it's got to the point where it should be excluded, because there's no probative value that can be attached to it and the Defence shouldn't be required to ask questions or put forth a defence in a case like that when the conclusions are so far removed from the actual hard evidence that the witness has given. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President, very briefly. I should note also that the portion of the transcript - I believe it was on page 65 - to which Your Honour, the Presiding Judge, referred to just a moment ago, clearly we have a situation here where the witness has answered the question and then a follow-on question was asked which is in fact what prompted Mr. Bourgon to object. For the record, Mr. President, those questions concluded that part of the direct examination, so the Prosecution would simply like to call to the attention of the Chamber that those questions have been asked and answered. And I only have just a few questions remaining for the witness which have nothing to do with that specific subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. It is twenty-five past 5.00. We are going to retire to deliberate. But this is also going to be our next break. We will resume in 25 minutes and we will then continue until 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now resume. The Trial Chamber deliberated during the break, and we will now hand down our decision. With regard to the right the Prosecution has to put the question mentioned a minute ago to the witness. We'll decide on whether the witness's testimony should be rejected. As it is based on hearsay the Trial Chamber would like to remind you of the previous decision, according to which hearsay evidence is admissible providing that the witness indicates the source of the information and provides other clarifications, other explanations with regard to the information concerned. In this particular case, the witness could not tell us about the sources, how it is that he knew the Mujahedin were the spearhead of the 7th Brigade and, as a result, of the 3rd Corps. And the Trial Chamber, if it gives probative value to the witness's answers, should ask the witness about the sources that allow him to claim that the Mujahedin spearheaded the attacks. When this is done, we will decide on the probative value of the answers provided. Without wasting any further time, I will ask the usher to call the witness into the courtroom so that I can ask him these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, we'll continue where we left off. As you heard, a minute ago, a while ago there was an objection to one of the answers that you provided. To enable the Trial Chamber to determine what the probative value of your answer is, I would like to ask you some questions in order to determine the basis on which you came to the conclusion that the Mujahedin were the 7th Brigade's spearhead and as a result they were the 3rd Corps's spearhead. You answered a question that was a general question, and you spontaneously started to speak about the fact that they spearheaded it. In military terms, what made you claim that the Mujahedin represented the spearhead, spearheaded the attacks? Is this an inference of yours, or is your claim based on specific facts, military intelligence, facts that concern attending meetings, command meetings? Is it based on reports? What exactly allows you to make such a claim? Could you answer my question, please.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the evidence that I gave came from the -- the briefings that we were given from our own military information cell. After we first encountered the foreign Mujahedin, our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could you just stop there. You mentioned a military information cell. Perhaps you could explain to us how these cells function, because this hasn't been mentioned yet. So you had a military information cell. Could you please tell us how this functions, unless it's a secret. But if not, you could perhaps provide us with some explanations.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Normally, as far as the military is concerned, information of that nature will be called "intelligence." But because we were working for the United Nations, it was called "military information," as a less overt term for what nevertheless was intelligence. In each battalion, we had a military information cell, which was commanded by a captain, and with a specialist staff sergeant, a senior non-commissioned officer from our intelligence corps, i.e., someone who was not -- who was a professional intelligence gatherer and collator and a small number of gatherers, eight or ten, who were involved in the gathering and soldiers of information. And their job was to learn as much about the various warring factions as possible, both as much as they could learn about the personalities commanding the various organisations, the way in which those organisations were organised, the weapons and equipment that they had, the tactics that they used on operations, and any other information such as dress, equipment, rank badges, and that sort of information. All of this information was collated by the military information cell and then each evening at 6.00 the hierarchy of the battalion, including myself as a company commander, would be given an intelligence briefing from the military information cell as to what had been discovered by the various elements of the battle group within the last 24 hours, and also what things we should be looking out for. Each patrol we were sent on had some form of military information purpose to it. So even if we were escorting a convoy, we would be briefed by the military information staff while we were in a particular village to find out some information that they required. And it is from these briefings that the information on the foreign Mujahedin was given to us by our military intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you received this information, but we can see how the information system functioned now. But how did this information show that there was an attack force that spearheaded attacks? How did this information allow one to say that the Mujahedin were the 3rd Corps's spearhead? Do you remember when exactly this was first mentioned and in relation to what sort of situation or what sort of event?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: After I met with the foreign Mujahedin on the 15th of May, this was the first that our -- our battalion had heard of these people in our area, and it then became part of our -- our patrol task was to find out as much about these people as possible. So when we went to various areas, one of the questions that would be tasked to ask various people were, "What are these people doing here? What is their role," then. I can only speak for myself. We asked this question to a number of people in villages, both Muslim and Croat villages, and the information I was told by villagers was that this was their role. This was then passed on to the military information cell, who had information from other patrols, of which there were very many, and that led them to the conclusion that this was how these -- these people were being used. On the briefing that we were given, we were given a variety of reasons why these soldiers were used in this particular role. And one was because they were better trained and more aggressive. The second reason was because they were foreign and, therefore, perhaps there was an element of expendability about them. And the third reason was that their mere presence and perceived fanaticism was guaranteed to make those HVO soldiers perhaps without the stomach to fight run away before a shot had been fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I have understood you correctly, it was only after the 15th of May that your battalion realised that there was this problem. As of the 15th of May, you tried to collate information of various kinds. You said that you had contact with Muslims and Croats and you obtained information from them. Your captain, the sergeant, and eight or ten soldiers also collated this information, and you put all these various elements together and came to the conclusion that this force spearheaded attacks. And you said that it was because they were better trained than others. You said they were more aggressive and that as they were foreigners, they were expendable in combat. This didn't pose a problem for the local inhabitants. And these are the reasons that you evoked.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Correct, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now continue after having heard your explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, earlier this afternoon you told us about your first encounter with General Hadzihasanovic and mentioned that you subsequently saw him on two or three other occasions and also on one social occasion. Is -- is that an accurate reflection of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Other than the social occasion, that is, the two or three occasions other than the one that you told us about at length earlier, do you recall the approximate dates or months when you met with General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact dates, but they would have been in the first two months of the tour. And as I recall, I met him in 3 Corps headquarters, once again asking for a piece of paper to be allowed to go through a checkpoint. And I also carried him in my vehicle on his way to a conference which had been brokered by Colonel Alastair Duncan.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: On how many occasions in total did you go to General Hadzihasanovic asking for a piece of paper to be allowed through a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Definitely two that I can remember. The incident which I've described and another incident later on in the tour, where we were stopped at a checkpoint on the road to two villages called Putis and Jelinak there. And the local BiH commander refused to let us through and I eventually went to see the general to get a piece of paper to go through this particular checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And Major, what was the result on this second occasion of getting a piece of paper from General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: We were, again, allowed to proceed through this checkpoint and to carry on with our task, only to be stopped later on at another checkpoint. But we'd given the first piece of paper away at this stage, so we had to go back through the procedure again. By this time, it was too late; it was getting dark, so we didn't go back to the corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Kent-Payne.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time there are no further questions by the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Without wasting any more time, I'll now turn to the Defence. We have another 50 minutes. I don't know whether that will be enough. We will perhaps have to continue tomorrow. But the Defence knows how much time they need. The Defence may now take the floor, but I would also like to point out that the Trial Chamber will have a few technical questions to put to the witness afterwards. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Major Kent-Payne. My name is Edina Residovic, and I represent General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, given the position that the major held at the time, the time which is relevant from the point of view of the indictment, and for the defence of General Hadzihasanovic, I'm going to put a lot of questions to the witness that have to do with the general context, after which I will ask the major some questions is that relate to the testimony he has given today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ask the witness all the questions you like, but ask the major brief questions so that the witness is not disoriented. Try to go stage by stage when putting your questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll follow your instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Major, today you met the lawyer Stephane Bourgon, who is co-counsel in General Hadzihasanovic's Defence team; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of May, 2000, you were questioned by the investigator --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no answer. We haven't heard the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, could you please answer aloud. You nodded, but this does not appear in the transcript. So I will ask you the same question again: Would it be correct to say that you met the lawyer Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel for General Hadzihasanovic? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct to say that in May 2000 you gave a statement to the an investigator from the OTP and you signed that statement? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that statement, you said that you had only mentioned things that you were familiar with and that were true in your opinion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from my colleague, you said that you have served in the British Army since 1977.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In April 1993, you were assigned tasks in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You were sent on a mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You and the Prince of Wales Regiment and with BritBat and UNPROFOR, you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Prior to going there, you spent a short period of time in Central Bosnia in February 1993, when you were part of the reconnaissance detachment mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes. We spent approximately five or six days in February 1993 on the reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The mission you were on in February 1993 was led by high-ranking officers from the Prince of Wales Regiment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to Bosnia and Herzegovina, you held the rank of a major in the British Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And today you also hold the rank of a major in the British Army.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Prior to this mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina - and this is the conclusion we can reach from -- on the basis of your professional experience - you had experience in areas of conflict.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Prior to going to Bosnia-Herzegovina, my experience of conflict was in Northern Ireland, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were a member of the regular army there, and they did not perceive armed groups in Northern Ireland as friendly groups but they perceived them as an enemy army; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. The way that the British government has dealt with the terrorist situation in Northern Ireland is to treat the terrorists as criminals and not members of a formed armed body. In this instance, they do not apply the Geneva Convention and the -- the terrorists, if they are caught, are tried in a criminal court, as opposed to a military court. That is the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The difference consisted in the fact that this was the first time that you were in an area where there was a war raging.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: That is -- that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And similarly, you hadn't any -- you hadn't had any experience, as far as the work of United Nations protection forces was concerned, in other countries.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During your brief stay in February and afterwards, when preparing to go to Bosnia in April, you had a few meetings to gain information about the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We had a series of training courses, which were run both at our base in Germany and at a military training area. And on this course, we were lectured by specialists who were flown over from Bosnia, both from the International Community and also from the Cheshire Regiment, who we were to replace.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At those training courses, you received information about the situation in the field as well as about the tasks you were to have and your mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before those training courses, while performing your duties in the British Army, you weren't in the situation -- you didn't have the opportunity of gaining more detailed information about Bosnia and Herzegovina and about the events that happened there or were happening there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: No, that's not true. Part of the training that we had was given to us by our specialist military training officers, and as part of this they gave us lengthy explanations as to the -- the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina, both before and after the break-up of the former Yugoslavia to enable all ranks to put into perspective the job that we were going to be doing and to give us some understanding of the context of the conflict and the various parties in that conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by the Prosecution, you said that you arrived there before your company; that is to say, you arrived in Bosnia around the 15th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After your company arrived on the 6th of May, 1993, you replaced the Cheshire Regiment that left Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 11th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: That's -- that's not entirely true. The change-over between regiments does not go everyone arriving on one day and everyone from a regiment disappearing the next day. It took place over several weeks. The date which is important is the handover of command from one regiment to another, which was the 11th of May. After the 11th of May, there was still some Cheshire soldiers remaining for three or four days there, but the majority had departed. But our official handover date was the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your colleagues from the Cheshire Regiment during the handover briefed you about your mission but also they told you about the events that had taken place during their stay in the territory covered by your regiment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes, they gave us an -- a concentrated briefing on what had taken place throughout the whole of their tour and also during the period of our handover, which as I explained earlier was some three weeks, they took us around many of the -- the areas and indeed showed us where some of the incidents had taken place, to give us a better feel for the background to the -- both the incidents and to the aftermath of these incidents, which we as the next battalion would be having to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Their information was very detailed, very thorough, very complete. You were thus in the position to continue the mission that the previous regiment started. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes, we were in a position to continue, but the problem was that the information that the Cheshires had been able to gain was only pertinent to certain parts of the area. The majority of the area, particularly those villages off the main roads, they had not been able to visit due to the difficulty of getting up the narrow tracks, due to the -- due to the deep snow and the winter weather conditions. Therefore, we started with a basis of information but with a requirement to move out and away from the main tracks to find out what was going on in the more inaccessible parts of our region.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your mission was a peace-keeping mission of the United Nations. Before that, you had gained some information about the UNPROFOR mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: That's -- yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the importance and significance of the UNPROFOR mission, I would like to ask you several questions. This will allow all of us, including the Trial Chamber, to follow the events which were part of the mission that you were involved in. You were familiar with the fact that the Security Council established this mission in February 1992, that this was based on the Resolution, and that the mandate was for the mission to be active in the five republics of the former Yugoslavia. Were you familiar with that fact?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: We were briefed on the United Nations Security Council Resolution and on the mandate that had been given to -- to UNPROFOR. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The first mandate was relative to the events in the Republic of Croatia. However, in order to prevent the escalation of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the UNPROFOR forces came to Sarajevo at the beginning of 1992. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes. By -- by my interpretation of "UNPROFOR," then, our interest was more in the activities of the British Battalion, then, which was deployed to the Central Bosnia region in around October of 1992, then. I was aware that the initial deployment of the UNPROFOR headquarters and the UN focus was in Sarajevo but due to the security situation this was forced to move from there at some stage in 1992. We were briefed on this as background, but the majority of the briefings that we had were those that were pertinent to our particular area; in this case, Central Bosnia and the area of the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Major, that the UNPROFOR main mandate as of the year 1992 up to the time of your arrival was extended and was added to?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: That's correct. As I mentioned in my earlier testimony, the commanding officer of the Cheshire Regiment, Lieutenant Colonel Bob Stewart, carried out a military procedure which we call "mission analysis" to determine the exact nature of his task. What "mission analysis" means in layman's term is that the commander gives a mission, in this case to escort humanitarian aid convoys, but gives the commander the latitude to work out exactly how he's going to carry out this mission. And Colonel Stewart, followed on by Colonel Duncan, decided that the best way to do this was to ensure that the -- as far as possible area was as peaceful as possible and therefore the aid convoys could move freely around without being disrupted by one militia or another and without the need for a heavy escorting presence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Major, you have answered my next question; however, let's go one step back. The first UNPROFOR mandate was to provide security for the Sarajevo airport and the delivery of humanitarian aid via that route. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: You are -- you are asking me questions which are way above my pay grade here. I was a company commander in Bosnia, and my primary concern was the mission that was given to our individual battalion. Of course we had some understanding of where our battalion fitted into the larger UNPROFOR picture, but as far as we were concerned, our mission was to escort humanitarian aid convoys around the area of operation and that what went on in Sarajevo was not necessarily of any bearing on what we did in our own -- in our own area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Major, if you are not able to provide all of us with some facts about the extension and expansion of the UNPROFOR mandate, I'm not going to ask you such questions. I just wanted to see whether you're familiar with the fact that the UNPROFOR went from the first mandate to the second mandate. You were part of that at the end of the year 1992. That mandate was to provide security for the land delivery of humanitarian aid via the UN convoys, the Red Cross convoys, that it was also involved in the exchange of prisoners and the movement of civilians. Are you familiar with the fact that the at the end of the year 1992 this was also included in the second UNPROFOR mandate? These are the things that I've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes. But for us, as the second British Battalion there, the second mandate was our only mandate and therefore that was the only one that applied to us and that was the one which we were briefed on and which we briefed down to our soldiers and the one in which we trained to carry out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have just completed my questions about the role of the United Nations and the UNPROFOR in Bosnia. Is it true that the UNPROFOR, when it was given the mandate to escort humanitarian convoys, was still involved in a peace-keeping mission, however, it was given the green light to use fire in case they were attacked during their mission?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: That's correct. Each of us was given a -- what we call in the British Army a rules of engagement card, and this specified the -- the situations in which we could -- we could return fire against any of the warring parties. But basically in essence, this was -- if we were under immediate threat of life and we were being fired at by local forces and there was no other way to -- to remove ourselves from the situation, then we were allowed to return fire. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The mandate that we have just described was the mandate that was in place throughout your stay in Bosnia and Herzegovina; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, the -- the mandate did not change; although, as the area became more peaceful, then, and as we refined our procedures, there was less need to physically escort some of the convoys. But as far as I'm aware, the mandate remained the same throughout our tour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As I have just said, this completes my question put to you in order to explain the mission that you were involved in. You said that your regiment had three companies, two of which were stationed in Vitez or in the immediate vicinity of Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: That's correct. There were actually four companies, as I explained. One was attached from the light dragoon's regiment there. So there were actually four companies: Two in Vitez, one in Tuzla, and one in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you have said on direct, you were in Vitez. Throughout all this time, Vitez was under the control of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: As I understand it, that's not, again, entirely true. In the centre of Vitez was -- is an area known as Stari Vitez, and this remained a Muslim enclave within the -- within the Croat-dominated area throughout our tour. And despite several attempts from the HVO to attack and capture the area of Stari Vitez, they remained there throughout the duration of our tour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Stari Vitez, the Muslim population lived together with some troops of the BiH army, and within your mandate you often had to help these people in Stari Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is correct. We did take humanitarian aid convoys to Stari Vitez and also evacuate people who needed urgent hospital treatment from there to other hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout your stay there, you witnessed a number of obstructions that the HVO put against the UNPROFOR preventing them from carrying out their mandate with respect to that area of Vitez, known as Stari Vitez.
